newsitem.title: BOSNIA: SOCCER-FIFA CAUTIOUS ON BOSNIA PLAYING AT HOME.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-FIFA CAUTIOUS ON BOSNIA PLAYING AT HOME.

text.p: Bosnia played their first soccer international in Sarajevo's Kosevo Stadium on Wednesday but a top UEFA official hinted that it might be some time before they could play there regularly.

As far as opponents Italy were concerned, the friendly opened the doors for Bosnia to play regularly in their own national stadium and for the world body to recognise that the Bosnian capital was no longer dangerous.

Bosnia played their first nominally "home" qualifier for the 1998 World Cup against Croatia in the Italian city of Bologna and their next match against Greece on April 2 will also be in Bologna unless the Kosevo Stadium is cleared.
FIFA have previously refused to allow Bosnia to play official matches in Sarajevo on safety grounds.

Ernie Walker, chairman of UEFA's stadia committee and a former general secretary of the Scottish Football Association, told Reuters at the stadium that his mission was to assess more than just the suitability of the venue.
"They've obviously done considerable work on the stadium but there's a lot that still has to be done," he said.
One immediate point was the fact that the recently refurbished stadium, which hosted the opening ceremony for the 1984 Winter Olympics, is not an all-seater venue.
"For big international matches now it's seating only but the stadium has distinct possibilities," said Walker.
His main worry however was more general.
"You know, there's more to it than the stadium when you host big World Cup qualifying matches for example.
"Imagine that Germany or Spain or England or whoever was coming and you have the whole infrastructure to consider -- the airport, the hotels, the media facilities etc."

The Italians, the first foreign national team to visit Sarajevo since the end of the 44-month war that killed 10,000 of the city's inhabitants, were staying at the central Holiday Inn, located in what was once one of the most deadly areas.
The hotel is being refurbished but rooms still have no telephone lines and some other hotels -- such as the high-rise Bristol -- are devastated and derelict.
"These are matters which presumably will improve as each month passes now. Obviously there's been a hell of a lot done between the end of the war and now," said Walker.
He said he would be reporting back to UEFA after the weekend and would not be going to this week's FIFA meeting in Zurich which was expected to discuss Bosnia's situation.
"There'll be liason now between UEFA and FIFA in the light of the Italians' experience," he said. "But it's not a decision to make overnight."
Italy had no doubts about playing in Sarajevo.

"If everything goes well, and I'm sure it will, Italy will open the door for Bosnian teams to compete at home in UEFA Cup competition. This is the objective we are after," Italian Olympic Committee head Mario Pescante told Reuters.
"We would like the national team to carry on playing in Bologna but we think they have a right to play at home. I think life here is really getting back to normality," he said.
